meta.title: X3 · P7 · P9 — What the Row Burndown Actually Is
meta.description: Plain-language explainer of the three defect lanes in the NAAC voice system and what landed on 2026-07-05

props.title: X3, P7, P9 — three names for three kinds of lying
props.subtitle: Each lane is a class of defect where the scorecard said 'fine' and the radio reality said otherwise

props.content: The system is scored on one instrument: `just baseline` replays 1,546 individual radio exchanges (rows) and checks that the AI pilot heard the right thing, understood the right thing, read back the right thing, and asked the fake flight-management module (FMM) for authority at the right moments. X3, P7 and P9 are the three families of rows where that scorecard was wrong — each for a different structural reason. This page explains each one in radio terms, not code terms.

CONTEXT
props.title: What a 'row' is
props.subtitle: Four corpora, one scorecard. Every claim of progress must show zero movement on rows it didn't intend to touch.

props.title: 🛩 A1 — grounded scenarios
props.content: Full flights (taxi, departure, cruise, approach) authored from FAA sources, replayed turn by turn with synthesized ATC audio through real speech recognition.

props.title: 🎓 A2 — PlaneEnglish lessons
props.content: Training-app dialogues, hand-authored gold. Same pipeline, different source of truth. This is where P7's 11 wrongly-accepted pilot calls lived.

props.title: 📻 B1 — template rows, real ASR
props.content: Every individual FAA phrase (one per template row) spoken by TTS, transcribed by Whisper, then parsed. Tests one phrase at a time against real speech-recognition noise.

props.title: 📝 B2 — template rows, perfect text
props.content: Same phrases with perfect transcripts — isolates parsing defects from hearing defects. When B1 fails and B2 passes, the ear is the problem, not the brain.

props.label: LANE 1
props.title: X3 — every phrase gets its own end-to-end test
props.subtitle: 'Template rows' burndown · 24 of 26 intents closed in 6 ticks

props.content:
The phraseology library holds ~476 FAA phrase templates ('CROSS RUNWAY 10 AT BRAVO', 'MAINTAIN 170 KNOTS UNTIL JEVEY'…), each cited to a 7110.65/AIM page. X3's job: every one of those rows gets a generated full-pipeline test — synth the phrase, parse it, render the pilot's readback, check it against the row's own FAA-grounded answer. Before X3, 26 intents had rows with **no test at all** (a guard test failed because slot fixtures were missing) — meaning whole families of phrases were unverified.

Why it took six ticks instead of two: the test fixtures turned out to be **secretly coupled to the B-corpus audio pipeline** — the manifest generator imports the tests' slot values, so an innocent fixture edit in tick 2 silently invalidated seven rows' audio when tick 3 ran a spike, killing the whole B lane. Mapping and defusing that coupling was most of a day, and it's now written into the worker rules so it can't recur.

props.title: A months-old gold contradiction
props.content: A PlaneEnglish scenario named the echo template ('Number two for Runway two seven left…') as its own expected answer while its gold text demanded a bare 'Roger'. A fallback path had been masking the conflict — X3's new selector exposed it. Fixed at the source, per the lesson's own phraseology.

props.title: Pilot request rendered as ATC command
props.content: 'Request climb flight level two one zero' was parsing as an altitude INSTRUCTION and rendering an executable climb readback. A pilot asking for something must never come out of the system sounding like ATC ordered it. Fixed by parser priority — safety-relevant.

props.title: Readbacks got honest
props.content: Mayday/Pan-Pan now acknowledged instead of 'Say again'. Wind-shear caution no longer read back (you read back clearances, not advisories). Crossing readbacks include the taxi-to clause. Each change justified by the live-radio test.

props.label: LANE 2
props.title: P7 — authority was speaker-blind
props.subtitle: 'Who keyed the mic' — closed today, +21 rows

props.content:
Scenario scripts contain both sides of the radio conversation: turns where **ATC transmits** and turns where **the ownship pilot transmits** (the scripted call the pilot makes, like 'Chicago Center, November One Seven X-ray X-ray, request flight following'). Every turn already carries a `speaker` field saying which one it is.

The defect: our fake FMM treated some of those **pilot** transmissions as if they were ATC commands — it minted 'accept' authority from them. In the air that's nonsense: a pilot's own request commands nothing; authority flows from ATC to ownship, never from ownship's own mouth. Eleven gold rows had been stamped 'accept' during an old pass-rate push to hide this.

The fix was small because the plumbing mostly existed: the speaker field now travels with the command all the way to the FMM boundary, the FMM refuses to mint rules from pilot turns, and pilot-origin proposals are rejected fail-closed unless they're a reporting obligation (the one legitimate case — answering 'say souls on board').

after.text: accept (reporting obligation — the one legit case)

props.label: SCOPE CHECK
props.title: 'Keyed the mic' is scenario metadata — not pilot-voice handling
props.subtitle: Answering the purview question directly

props.content:
**We did not add pilot→COPI speech handling.** 'Who keyed the mic' = the `speaker: atc | pilot` field that every scripted scenario turn has always carried. P7 stopped that fact from being *dropped* on its way to the fake FMM, so pilot transmissions become authority-inert. It is the opposite of expanding into pilot speech: it makes the system formally deaf to pilot speech as a source of command authority.

**Prod is untouched by default.** The live radio pipeline transcribes received transmissions; the envelope's new origin field is optional, and no producer sets it — unset means 'unknown', which behaves exactly as before. The change list for the P7 commit is modules/types, modules/intent, harness, tests. **Zero gateway, zero Communication-Dashboard, zero COPI GUI code.**

The demo GUI's pilot-speech subset (the Windows console buttons, because you can't fly MSFS and press buttons simultaneously) remains a demo-only lane. If any of it ever needs to feed this pipeline, the Gateway Authority Boundary applies: catalogue in SUNNY_SIDECAR.md, feature-flag, no independent authority.

props.label: LANE 3
props.title: P9 — the scorer rewards deafness on broadcasts
props.subtitle: Grounding done today · scorer redesign queued behind corpus work

props.content:
When a radio call is **not addressed to ownship** — another aircraft's traffic call, an ATIS loop, 'ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT' — the scorer currently passes the turn if we parsed **nothing**. A system that goes deaf on the party line scores identically to one that builds a correct traffic picture. That's `intent_match = not observed.intent` at turn_score.py:509.

In the air, every broadcast must be *understood* even when it must not be *answered*: an overheard MAYDAY literally commands radio silence while requiring you to track who's in trouble; a fuel-dumping broadcast means avoid that area; an ATIS letter gets acknowledged later, on first contact, never on the ATIS frequency. Exactly one class crosses into command authority: all-aircraft operational directives (the grounded example is gate-hold: 'ALL AIRCRAFT CONTACT ground ON…'), and only when ownship is in the directed class.

Before touching the scorer, the taxonomy had to exist — the full 8-class table with verbatim FAA citations now lives in **MISSING_BROADCAST.md at the repo root**, and the 5-step execution queue is in `.lev/scratch/20260705-ratchet-burndown-p9-broadcast.yaml`. The blocker discovered: four classes have **zero corpus coverage**, and 29 existing 'All aircraft' turns are invented filler ('pattern stabilizing, nice work everyone') — scoring against those would make the new surface green by vacuity.
